summary: Milwaukee's North Point light: 1855 brick tower, 1888 cast-iron octagon, raised 1912-13; keeper Georgia Stebbins served 1874-1907; museum open weekends.

structures.note: 39 ft to top of ventilator ball in 1888 (HAER); 36.25 ft to lantern centre (USLHS)
Replaced and moved about 100 ft inland in 1888 (HAER). The museum gives it as 28 ft.

access.note: Museum open to the public for tours on Saturdays and Sundays, 1 to 4 p.m.; closed dates on the museum's site.

facts.agency: North Point Lighthouse and Museum (North Point Lighthouse Friends, Inc.)

events.note: Brick tower built to mark the entrance into the Milwaukee River
Original brick tower replaced and moved about 100 feet inland because of bluff erosion
Present octagonal cast-iron tower and keeper's quarters opened
Propeller James Fisk, Jr. stranded half a mile north of North Point, 29 July 1880

Gale washed away the house on the crib of the new city waterworks tunnel off Milwaukee, 19-20 April 1893: all but one of the men drowned; the survivor was rescued by the Milwaukee station's crew, towed by the tug Welcome (LSS 1893). The Service's medal list gives 'fifteen men'; WMHS gives sixteen trapped and fifteen dead
Light discontinued 30 June 1907 (keeper's final log entry)
Congress appropriates $10,000 to raise the light
Contract for raising the light approved; work began July 1912
Light displayed in the raised structure from 15 December 1912
Raising completed April 1913 at a cost of $9,455
Coast Guard takes over the lighthouses from the Lighthouse Service
Decommissioned; discontinued 1994 per USLHS and the museum
North Point Lighthouse Friends, Inc., formed to restore the station
Restoration completed in the fall of 2007

corrections.proposed: original brick tower 1855; cast-iron octagon 1888, 11.0 m (36 ft to lantern centre)
corrections.why: HAER says the 1855 tower was brick and the cast-iron octagon was built in 1888 at 39 feet to the ventilator ball. USLHS gives 36.25 feet to the lantern centre.
USLHS gives the light at 122 feet above mean high water (37.2 m). The 47 m figure is not found in any source read for this story; confirm before changing.
No source read for this story dates a build in 1879. HAER gives 1855 and 1888 for the two towers.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1855 and 1888 as first-lit years. The first light was 1855 (USLHS; HAER). 1888 is the present tower's year, given by the museum and the Milwaukee Notebook as when the present lighthouse opened.

Daniel K. Green: roster 1871-1881, museum list 1871-1874. Georgia Stebbins: arrived 1873 (museum, WMHS) or January 1874 (her 1897 words via the Milwaukee Notebook); official keeper July 1881 (roster, museum, WMHS). Reynold W. Johnson: roster 1924-1928, museum list 1924-1940. The story gives the sources' dates.

The museum gives the tower as 74 feet; the USLHS record gives 36.25 feet to the lantern centre; HAER gives 39 feet to the ventilator ball. The story uses HAER and USLHS figures and does not repeat the museum's 74 feet.
The roster has Eli Bates (1838-1848); the museum list has Eli Jr. (1836-1848). The roster begins before the 1855 light. No source read explains the earlier keepers.

The museum says Olmsted conceived the park in 1893; the NRHP Lake Park nomination says arrangements began in 1892 and the Olmsted plan dates from 1895. The story uses the nomination's 1892 and does not repeat the 1893 date.

resolved_conflicts.field: waterworks crib disaster, 20 April 1893 (count of men)
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Life-Saving Service's 1893 report and medal list say fifteen men were in the crib and all but one drowned. The WMHS article says sixteen were trapped and fifteen died. The story gives both counts and does not choose.

notes_for_editor: The 1893 waterworks crib disaster is now sourced to the Life-Saving Service's 1893 report (casualty table, scan page 143; gold medal list, scan page 201). The report says fifteen men (medal list) and all but one drowned; WMHS says sixteen trapped and fifteen dead. The telephone detail (Mrs. Stebbins ran to a telephone) rests on WMHS alone. A Chronicling America search for the crib disaster in Wisconsin papers, 1893, returned no hits. The roster's pre-1855 keepers (from 1838) are not explained by any source read here, and the story does not describe them. The Lighthouse Board's 1892 entry 1242 is headed 'Milwaukee, Lake Michigan, Wisconsin' and describes the light-house reservation; it is identified with North Point by its position and by the Board's account of the station, not by name (scan page 500). Ownership of the tower is not stated by any source read; the HAER form names the Coast Guard as owner in 1979 and the museum runs the site. The museum's 74-foot tower height conflicts with the HAER 39 feet to the top of the ventilator ball and the USLHS 36.25 feet to the lantern centre; the story gives the museum figure as the museum's own. The period between the 1907 discontinuance and the 1912-13 relighting is not documented in the sources read. The museum's keeper list includes post-1960 Coast Guard personnel; they are not named in the story. The 1897 Milwaukee Journal words come through the Milwaukee Notebook, and the story footnotes the blog, not the newspaper. The 1893 medal list does not name the surfman's station; the casualty table names the Milwaukee station's crew for the rescue. Wikipedia was used for leads only and is not cited. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the 1892 Board entry (scan p. 500) is headed only 'Milwaukee, Lake Michigan, Wisconsin'; its light-house reservation, present light-house and park details match North Point, and the story now says so. The museum's own pages give three tower heights (74 ft on the About page; 28 ft original and 39 ft for the 1888 tower on the Georgia page); the story states the conflict. The Lake Park date conflict (museum 1893 for Olmsted's design; NRHP nomination 1892 for the start of arrangements) is now stated in the story. The Olsen medal row (surfman, gold medal, May 24, 1893) was also checked against the archive.org page image (scan p. 201, printed p. 198).
